text: Found and resolved the issue. The newish `arraymap` primitive has an expanding head, but was never previously read past it's limit due to the nature of the confirmation prevout query that consumed it. I changed two more tables to arraymap (`validated_bk` and `txs`) and in these cases the tables are read for items that may not be found just due to lack of ordering. When the element searched is greater than the head allocation there is a read protection fault. When writing there is no problem because a write would just expand the head. The low level file does not guard against such overflows, because at such a low level that's a big performance expense for all tables, most of which wouldn't benefit from it. The `arrayhead` test cases didn't cover it, because they were derived from the `hashmap` tests, and `hashhead` doesn't resize. So test added, simple fix within the `arrayhead`. <https://github.com/libbitcoin/libbitcoin-database/pull/629>

elements.text:
These arraymaps are good for block-indexed tables, since the array head is small (<1M) vs. tx (>1B) and input/output (>2.6B). The array head can be thought of as a simple hashmap head with a fixed 1.0 load factor, and pass-thru hash function. Each bucket holds the singular element body position. This means that repeat entries for the same element get overwritten in the head and are essentially hidden in the body. This works well for state transitions where there is one state per header, and prevouts and txs association, where there is only one set per header/block.

The arraymap heads are larger (e.g. than a 2.2 LF hashhead), but they are sequential, so more efficient paging, and the arraymap requires no keys or links within the body - so the tables are overall much smaller and also with less paging. The mapping allows elements to be written out of order and yet indexed with array efficiency (always O(1)).

elements.text: Completed the last open issue. The entire stack is essentially lock-free, with synchronization primitives buried in C++ std lib (concurrent loops), ASIO, ZeroMQ, and our store primitives. But I used a simple
std::mutex
with
std::unique_lock

to synchronize between the candidate chain and confirmed chain. Basically we cannot allow popping of blocks from the candidate chain during the organization of blocks into the confirmed chain, since the candidate chain provides order for the confirmed chain.

It would be possible to push this into a store atomic read of the full candidate branch, which hash the slight drawback of holding this set in a redundant temporary structure during organization. This would have to be captured before determining if the branch is strong. There would be a very small performance hit, but that would allow the implementation to not expose any synchronization primitives at the application layer.

text:
Completed the last open issue. The entire stack is essentially lock-free, with synchronization primitives buried in C++ std lib (concurrent loops), ASIO, ZeroMQ, and our store primitives. But I used a simple `std::mutex` with `std::unique_lock` to synchronize between the candidate chain and confirmed chain. Basically we cannot allow popping of blocks from the candidate chain during the organization of blocks into the confirmed chain, since the candidate chain provides order for the confirmed chain.

It would be possible to push this into a store atomic read of the full candidate branch, which hash the slight drawback of holding this set in a redundant temporary structure during organization. This would have to be captured before determining if the branch is strong. There would be a very small performance hit, but that would allow the implementation to not expose any synchronization primitives at the application layer.

elements.text: On the call today I mentioned that we are now precomputing (1)
success
opcode, (2)
invalid
opcode, and (3)
op_roll
existence in all scripts during parse. This includes reading off the wire and from the store, though it's very efficient since the iteration is already necessary. Previously we were only testing for
invalid
during parse, and
op_roll
was computed on the fly prior to script execution. This saved one bit (
bool
) per script, which wasn't really worth it, since the two flags would just be packed into one byte by the compiler. And since we otherwise need another iteration for the
success
codes prior to tapscript execution, it was an easy choice to just put these all into the script parser, which basically looks like this (emplace invokes
chain::op(reader)
to perform an in-place construction on the
operation
stack).
I also mentioned that because we can't really know if it will be executed as tapscript at the parse point, we record these for all scripts. But since the definition of
invalid
opcode has changed (reduced to just
op_verif
and
op_vernotif
in tapscript) and the unconditional
success

codes apply only in tapscript, it seemed that this would present some complexity and require additional parse results.

But it turns out that above is all that is required. The last set of comments here explains how it works out, which was quite elegant.
The above code is invoked at the very beginning of the
interpreter::run()
method, which runs the script:
I wrote this up in the comments, but basically I decided not to do anything regarding the supposedly new
op_success
codes. None are renamed, it's just another method to test whether a code is in the unconditional success category, and one invocation of that test in the above
initialize()
method. Otherwise nothing changes, and the codes retain their previous state (invalid or reserved) in non-tapscript executions. So just as there are no actual
op_invalid
codes, and no
op_conditional
codes, and some reserved codes that are not named
op_reserved
, unconditional success is just a new category - confused by the BIP presentation.

text: I wrote this up in the comments, but basically I decided not to do anything regarding the supposedly new `op_success` codes. None are renamed, it's just another method to test whether a code is in the unconditional success category, and one invocation of that test in the above `initialize()` method. Otherwise nothing changes, and the codes retain their previous state (invalid or reserved) in non-tapscript executions. So just as there are no actual `op_invalid` codes, and no `op_conditional` codes, and some reserved codes that are not named `op_reserved`, unconditional success is just a new category - confused by the BIP presentation.

elements.text:
This clears up the questions I had on duplexing.

Our p2p operates over TCP which is full duplex, but the semantics of the protocols are more like half duplex, where there is a request/response, even though either party can initiate and one party can simply broadcast to the other (like tx announcements).

HTTP is the same, I don't see any reason the implementation would be affected. But interestingly, WebSockets can also be implemented on the same stack, since it's just a different semantic. IOW we can broadcast from a notification subscriber over the socket, and the client can also spend requests.

One limitation that we presently have on the vc++ builds is that there are no ARM boost NuGet packages. Otherwise I would update the two that I maintain (secp256k1 and libzmq). elements.text: I ran into a boost ARM bug in our latest version, where boost was invoking Intel intrinsics whenever that specific header is present, but the header is always present on ARM as well. No way to fix that except to upgrade, so I started at boost latest (1.87) and that has a problem in the NuGet packages (one unresolved external in the std lib) so I dropped down to 1.86 and it all looks good.

elements.text: It looks like ARM vectorization is active and successful on CI via macOS. Really just came down to defining for ARM the same set of intrinsics wrappers that we have for Intel (below). The sha template just picks up this vs. the Intel version. And this file was entirely generated by Grok, with some minor fixes and cosmetics from me.

ARM Neon is the common intrinsics library (there's a newer one but not widely deployed). This usually includes SHA intrinsics, but is limited to 128 bit vectorization. On Intel we get 128, 256, and 512 with newer machines, as well as SHA (which often is not present). The 128 bit vectorization helps when SHA is not present, but it's usually present with Neon. And native SHA is much faster, so more important to get that incorporated. That's a similar process, though the semantics of the intrinsics differ between ARM and Intel, so it's not quite as straightforward to get a clean common implementation.

elements.text: I also did a custom software implementation of intrinsics that Intel doesn't provide but are necessary to round out the vectorization library. Specifically that gives us the ability to vectorize sha512 on 32 bit builds. Obviously not the highest priority, but not a lot of work and cleans up some code. Unfortunately it's not quite done, as I have native sha512 test failures across the board on 32 bit Intel. It's probably good on 32 bit ARM with Neon, because those are all natively implemented, but I have no test platform for that.
